# Powdery mildew on leaves

Powdery mildew appears as white or grey talc-like patches on the upper surfaces of leaves, first as scattered spots, then as a film covering whole leaves. Cucumbers, squash, courgettes, roses and peas are frequent hosts. Unlike most fungal diseases it thrives in warm dry conditions with high humidity around the leaf surface — dense shaded foliage without rain is the classic setup, so an overwatered bed is not required.

Remove and bin the worst-affected leaves rather than composting them; the fungus overwinters on debris. Improving airflow is the cheap fix: space plants farther apart, prune crowded growth and avoid working among plants while they are wet. On susceptible crops pick resistant varieties next season.

For treatment, a homemade spray of one part milk to nine parts water, applied weekly in sunlight, suppresses the fungus on cucumbers and squash. A half-teaspoon of baking soda per liter of water with a drop of soap raises leaf pH against it, but test on a few leaves first since strong solutions burn. Potassium bicarbonate sprays are the horticultural-grade version of the same idea. Sulfur dust works but harms beneficial insects and burns leaves above 30 degrees. Spraying after infection spreads is much less effective than starting at the first spots, so inspect the undersides of lower leaves weekly in midsummer.
